A1.justification: The renamed dataset, retained prompting strategies, and matching experiments identify the same research work. All supplied pages are readable, including figures, tables, equations, and v4's Appendices A–G. v1 contains no appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original human preference annotations, MLLM evaluations, prompting and voting experiments, and model-ranking results in Sections 3–4.

after.justification: v4 reports original preference annotations, benchmark and ensemble experiments, and MER2025 submission rankings. Appendix G supplies additional per-strategy results.

M1.justification: v1 Section 2 binarizes aggregate pairwise preferences before fitting Bradley–Terry; v4 Section 5 and Appendix F instead fit win/loss/tie counts with an explicit tie parameter. Crowdsourcing also changes from filtering models above 60% on both metrics to recognition-ranked top-k voting. The four underlying S1–S4 prompting procedures are retained.

E1.justification: The preference benchmark retains the 1,368 starting videos, three-annotator consensus rule, and matching agreement results under its new name; naming MERR-Fine, MER-Caption+, and MER2024 adds provenance information. However, v4 replaces the ranking demonstration with MER2025 submissions without describing its video pool sufficiently to establish whether data coverage differs from v1's 332-sample demonstration.

E2.justification: AffectGPT is removed from the main comparison. The order-combination experiment changes from 18 models in v1 Figure 12 to 14 open-source models in v4 Figure 9: all six closed-source models and AffectGPT disappear, while Qwen2.5-Omni, VITA-1.5, and LLaVA-Next-Video join that comparison. Qwen3-8B also disappears from the external-LLM comparison.

E3.justification: The default external LLM changes from Qwen3-14B to Qwen2.5-7B, affecting S3/S4 settings. v4 adds ensemble protocols comparing unrestricted, open-source, and closed-source pools, with and without normal-swapped aggregation. Multi-run consistency is dropped, and the practical ranking experiment uses competition submissions instead of v1's ten named models.

E4.justification: v4 adds description-vocabulary analysis, explicit metric-correlation analyses, and ensemble studies separating model-pool restrictions, order aggregation, recognition performance, and swap robustness. Its external-LLM analysis compares effects across individual MLLMs, replacing v1's aggregate three-LLM plots. The earlier multi-run consistency analysis is removed.

E5.justification: v4 Figure 8 adds explicit Pearson-correlation estimation across all versus best prompting strategies, replacing v1's qualitative correlation discussion. Repeated-run uncertainty reporting remains unchanged: both versions specify two runs and report means and standard deviations, without adding confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Numerous S3/S4 results and selected strategies change. For example, Qwen2-Audio's best-listed two-class WAF changes from 60.42 with S3 to 63.17 with S4 under the revised external-LLM setting; this is not a same-setting gain. Qwen2.5-Omni retains 67.21 and becomes the highest remaining entry after AffectGPT's 68.90 is removed. v4 also adds full-strategy, correlation, ensemble, and competition-ranking results.

T1.justification: The formal ranking model receives a localized but substantive revision: v1's binary preference likelihood is replaced by three-outcome probabilities and a count-weighted likelihood with tie parameter beta in v4 Appendix F. No new theorems or proofs appear. The explicit swap-consistency formula describes the existing flip-consistency concept.

C1.justification: v1 presents a novel ground-truth-free ranking strategy as its primary contribution, with automatic preference prediction supporting it. v4 centers its contributions on understanding emotion preferences through EmoPrefer-Data and EmoPrefer-Bench, relegating ranking to a practical application and adding prospective relevance to emotion-aware reward models.

C2.justification: v4 replaces the rationale favoring Qwen3-14B with evidence supporting Qwen2.5-7B and the interpretation that larger LLMs need not align better with human preferences. It adds ensemble-specific robustness and cost interpretations and explicit zero-shot and descriptive-emotion limitations. Conversely, it drops v1's strong qualification that automatic rankings are only references and reliable rankings still require human annotation.

D1.justification: v4 newly documents dataset provenance, annotator recruitment, the 12-item screening test and 75% threshold, and word-extraction prompts. It specifies a dataset license and reports provision of data, code, and intermediate outputs in supplementary materials, with a planned public release. However, v1's explicit final dataset size of 574 and detailed ranking sample budget are no longer supplied.

R1.justification: v4 positions human pairwise preference evaluation as prior MER2025 work rather than its principal novelty. Appendix B substantially expands discussion of categorical, dimensional, and descriptive emotion representations, LLM judges, reward models, and verifiers. Table 1 adds VL-RewardBench, MM-RLHF, and Multimodal RewardBench while removing EvalBiasBench; these are literature comparisons, not newly evaluated baselines.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statements, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around EmoPrefer. The document is reorganized into dataset, metrics, benchmark, and application sections, with prompting templates and ranking mathematics moved into appendices. Related-work, limitations, ethics, and reproducibility sections expand the narrative substantially.

P2.justification: v4 redraws the evaluation overview and adds a pipeline diagram, word clouds, correlation heatmaps, expanded ensemble plots, and a comprehensive appendix results table. Existing prompting figures move to appendices, the annotation screenshot is cartoonized, and several multi-panel experiments are redesigned. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: v4 improves transparency through explicit dataset provenance and annotator screening, complete per-strategy results in Appendix G, and more informative ensemble analyses. These make the benchmark easier to inspect and its recommendations better supported. The unexplained removal of AffectGPT, omission of the final dataset count, and weaker caution about automated rankings offset part of that benefit, leaving a modest overall improvement.
